angle: Treat AI regulation as product requirements per market, not philosophical noise.
sourceTitle: The Different Philosophies Driving AI Regulation Today
linkedinPost:
If your AI program has one policy for “compliance,” you don’t have a policy. You have a risk.

Knowledge at Wharton lays out how the U.S., EU, and others are approaching AI regulation with very different philosophies. I see this play out in enterprise deployments weekly.

Leaders hope for a single global standard. Instead, we have patchwork reality: purpose-based rules in one market, process-based in another, data-locality and high‑risk use restrictions elsewhere. Waiting for convergence delays value—and compounds remediation costs later.

My take: treat regulation like product requirements by market. Encode it into your architecture and ops. Concretely: build a catalog of use cases with risk tiers, map controls (data provenance, human oversight, redress) per tier, log model lineage, and make consent, routing, and retention configurable by region.

One customer saved months by separating “policy as code” from the model layer—so when the EU tightened high‑risk definitions, they updated guardrails without retraining.

Question for leaders: do you know which markets you’re compliant in today—and could you prove it in a week if asked? #AIStrategy #AIAdoption #EnterpriseAI #DigitalTransformation
xPost: Stop hoping for one AI rulebook. Treat regulation as product requirements per market: use-case tiers, policy-as-code, regional routing, and auditable lineage. Prove compliance in a week, not a wishlist. #AIStrategy #EnterpriseAI
